title: C memory: the stack and the heap
summary: Where your variables live, why malloc needs free, and what a leak or a stack overflow is.

text: A running program gets its memory in parts. Two of them matter every day:
- the stack, for the variables of your functions;
- the heap, for memory you ask for yourself.

scheme: int add(int a, int b) { int s = a+b; return s; }
text: - Each call gets a box on the stack, a frame, with its arguments and local variables.
- A call inside a call adds a new box below it: on Linux PCs the stack grows down, toward lower addresses.
- The newest box is still called "the top of the stack": top means the last one added, not the highest.

scheme: add has returned: its box is gone,
a, b and s don't exist anymore
text: When a function returns, its box is thrown away. Nobody has to free it: it's automatic.
- That's why the stack is fast and easy.
- And why returning the address of a local variable is a bug: it points into a box that no longer exists.
A function that calls itself stacks one box per call.
- Without a base case (a case that returns without calling itself again), the boxes pile up.
- The stack is small (8 MB by default on Linux): it overflows and the program crashes.
malloc asks for memory on the heap and gives you its address.
- p is a pointer: a small variable, on the stack, that holds that address.
- The heap memory stays after the function returns, until you free it.
- malloc returns NULL when it can't give memory: always check it before use.

scheme: free(p);  p still holds the old address
p = NULL;  nothing left to follow
text: free gives the memory back to malloc, which will reuse it for something else. But p still holds the old address: a dangling pointer.
- Using p after free is a "use after free" bug: it may work, crash, or corrupt data.
- p = NULL right after free makes a mistake crash at once, where you can find it. And free(NULL) does nothing, so a second free is harmless.

scheme: its box and p are gone    ▲ nobody points here
text: load returned without free: p is gone, the 100 bytes are not. Nobody can free them anymore. That's a memory leak.
- A program that leaks a little on each request grows until the system kills it.
- The rule: every malloc has exactly one free.
$ gcc -g -fsanitize=address prog.c -o prog && ./prog

scheme: who frees   automatic           you, with free
use it for  small, short-lived  big or long-lived
text: - A local variable goes on the stack: nothing to do.
- Big data, or data that must outlive the function: malloc, and one free later.
